intended_object: A family of scheme morphisms f_j : X_j → Y is jointly scheme-theoretically dominant when no proper closed subscheme of Y has every f_j factoring through it. Equivalently, the induced map ∐ X_j → Y is scheme-theoretically dominant: the intersection of the kernel ideal sheaves is zero. This is read off the docstring, the module doc and the companion theorem `jointlySchemeTheoreticallyDominant_iff_subscheme`; Milne Def. 1.15 is the special case where the family consists of field-valued points.
explanation:
The definition says the infimum, in the complete lattice `Y.IdealSheafData`, of the kernels `(f j).ker` is `⊥`. Mathlib defines scheme-theoretic dominance of a single morphism the same way: `IsSchemeTheoreticallyDominant f` means `f.ker = ⊥`. For a one-element family the two notions coincide, so this is the direct generalization to families.

Mathlib's `Hom.ker` is the largest quasi-coherent ideal sheaf through which f factors, i.e. the ideal of the scheme-theoretic image. A morphism f factors through V(I) exactly when I ≤ f.ker. So ⨅ ker f_j is the largest ideal I such that every f_j factors through V(I), and the condition says no proper closed subscheme contains all the f_j. That is the standard notion, and the file proves it in `jointlySchemeTheoreticallyDominant_iff_subscheme`. The same argument shows it is equivalent to scheme-theoretic dominance of the coproduct map, whenever that coproduct exists.

Edge cases behave correctly:
- For an empty family the infimum is ⊤, so the condition holds only when ⊤ = ⊥, i.e. when Y is empty. This matches the subscheme characterization.
- For non-quasi-compact maps, this ker-based version can differ from Stacks' "O_Y → ∏ f_j* O_{X_j} injective". It follows Mathlib's own convention for single morphisms, and the two agree in the quasi-compact cases the library uses.

The definition works for arbitrary schemes and arbitrary index types, so it is not too narrow. Mathlib has only the single-morphism notion, with no family version, so there is no exact counterpart.
